title: Representation-as-a-Judge: Small Models Evaluate via Hidden States
one_liner: Small language models can judge the quality of answers just by looking at their internal thoughts, without needing to write or speak.
lead: Evaluating answer quality usually means asking a big expensive language model to produce a written judgment. But this paper discovers something surprising: tiny models already know how to judge, hidden deep inside their layers. The paper turns this into a practical tool called INSPECTOR that listens to what small models think internally, rather than waiting for them to generate words out loud.

problem.h2: Judging answers is expensive and opaque
paras: Today, when we want to know if a model's answer is good, we ask a large language model to score it — the LLM-as-a-Judge approach. But large models are slow, costly, and their judgments are hard to understand or trust.

Why not use tiny models instead? They are fast and cheap. But tiny models are bad at writing — they stumble, they miss words, they make grammatical errors. People naturally assumed that if a model cannot write well, it cannot judge well either.

callout.html: Small models cannot judge well because they cannot generate good text.

panels.title: 1. Old way: ask a big model to write
panels.caption: Large judge writes: 'This answer is logically sound, fluent, and consistent.'

panels.title: 2. Small model's spoken words are messy
panels.caption: Small model writes: 'Answer is good... uhh... maybe fluent... not sure.'

panels.title: 3. But inside, it knows more than it says
panels.caption: Deep in layer 8, hidden neurons light up with judgment signals.

panels.title: 4. Extract those signals and train classifiers
panels.caption: A simple linear classifier learns to read the brain signals.

panels.title: 5. Tiny judge that works without speaking
panels.caption: INSPECTOR predicts scores as well as the big model, but runs 10x faster.

steps.text: Run a large language model judge on the same (prompt, answer) pair and get aspect scores like logicality, fluency, consistency (1–5 for each).
Feed the prompt and answer to a small model. Capture its internal layer-by-layer representations (the numbers in each neuron) as it reads through the text.
Test which layers inside the small model carry the strongest prediction signal for each aspect. Mid-to-upper layers usually work best.
Use simple linear classifiers on top of those layer signals to predict the aspect scores the large model gave.
For a new answer, extract representations from the small model and feed them through the trained classifiers to get fast, interpretable scores.

paras: Instead of asking the model to generate a judgment word-by-word (decoding), the paper reads the model's internal thoughts before any words come out.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Evaluative signal in layers
hidden.name: evaluative signal strength per layer
paras: This is the amount of evaluation-relevant information hiding in the neurons at each depth of the model. It is not visible in the model's written output, but it is there in the numbers. The paper measures it by training a simple classifier on each layer separately and measuring how well that layer alone can predict the aspect scores.

Mid-to-upper layers contain strong evaluative signals: a classifier trained on those layers can predict aspect scores with high accuracy. The output layer is weak because it is optimized for generation, not judgment. This shows that evaluation information builds up throughout the model, not just at the end.

heat.caption: Darker means the layer captures stronger judgment signals. Highlighted layers are most useful.

reads.html: The model builds up a sense of what makes a good answer as it reads deeper. This sense is much richer than what the model can put into words.
Per-layer probing classifiers show F1 score peaks in intermediate layers, indicating that semantic evaluation capacity accumulates throughout the network, independent of generation quality.

paras: Here is the core insight: evaluating an answer is an easier task than generating a good written judgment. Generating requires the model to know what words to pick, spell them correctly, construct grammar, and order them sensibly. Evaluating requires the model to recognize patterns of logicality, fluency, consistency — patterns that are much simpler.

Because evaluation is simpler, the model can solve it in its internal representations much earlier than in its external words. Mid-layer neurons start encoding judgment signals (logicality, fluency) as the model reads through the text. By the time the model reaches the output stage, those signals are still present in the intermediate layers, but they get drowned out because the output layer is optimized for word generation, not scoring.

INSPECTOR sidesteps generation entirely. It trains classifiers to read the mid-layer signals directly, before they are lost to the output process. Since those signals were built to solve a simpler task, they are cleaner and more reliable than the generated words.

math.words: For each aspect, a simple linear classifier takes the layer representations and outputs a score. For each response sample, extract the mean and last-token hidden representations from each layer, compute attention-entropy statistics, pool them, and concatenate features from selected layers.
symbols: the j-th extracted feature from layer representations
the learned importance of that feature
the default score before reading any features
hidden neuron values at selected layers as the model reads the text

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we extract 4 features from a small model: F1=3.2 (mean pooling from layer 7), F2=0.8 (attention entropy), F3=2.1 (last token norm), F4=1.5 (variance).
Rounded to 3-4 on a 1-5 scale. The large judge said 3, so INSPECTOR was close and fast.

math.note: The classifier simply reads the layer signals and outputs a number; it needs almost no computation compared to decoding words.

charts.title: Small model speaking (naive)
charts.note: A small model asked to score out loud is unreliable because it generates garbled words.

charts.title: INSPECTOR (this paper)
charts.note: By reading internal signals instead of waiting for words, INSPECTOR matches the large judge's accuracy while staying fast and cheap.

charts.title: Large language model judge
charts.note: Baseline: expensive and slow, but accurate if the judgment is correct.

items.b: The small model must see the answer.
items.html: INSPECTOR only works if the small model can encode judgment signals in its representations. If the task is too far outside what the small model was trained to understand, its layers will be silent. For example, a small model trained only on code may not encode judgments about poetry quality.

items.b: The large judge must be reliable.
items.html: The ground-truth scores come from the large judge. If the large judge is biased (e.g., always favors verbose answers), INSPECTOR will learn to copy that bias, not correct it.

items.b: Classifiers trained on imbalanced data may fail.
items.html: If the training data is imbalanced (mostly 5-star answers, few 1-star ones), the classifier learns to recognize good answers but struggles to spot bad ones. Downsampling helps by using equal numbers of each score, but it can lose some examples from scores that were rare.

items.b: Done right: use a balanced dataset.
items.html: Collect aspect-level scores across the full range (1-5) in equal amounts, or use downsampling during training to create balance. Validate on a test set with natural proportions to catch bias.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple evaluation task: collect 50 answers to a reasoning question (e.g., a math word problem from GSM8K). Ask a large language model to score each answer on fluency (1-5). Extract representations from a small model (e.g., Llama-2-7B) at layers 16, 20, 24 as it reads each answer. Train a linear classifier on 40 answers to predict the fluency score from layer 20 alone. Evaluate on the held-out 10 answers and report accuracy.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = (number of predictions within 1 point of large judge) / 10
demo.closing: The demo should show that the small model's mid-layer signals alone can match a large judge's judgment, without generating any words.
